meta.study: An Empirical Study on the Impact of String Interpolation on Program Readability and Comprehension
meta.description: Complete task inventory for the within-subjects experiment. Each participant saw all 16 tasks in a fixed order, alternating between Concatenation and Interpolation conditions. See TASK_DESIGN.md for the pseudo-syntax evaluation rules used to determine correct answers.

complexity_levels.L-1: Two embedded variables or literal values
complexity_levels.L-2: Three embedded variables or literal values
complexity_levels.L-3: Four embedded variables or literal values
complexity_levels.L-4: More than four embedded variables or literal values

notes: Complexity values recorded here reflect what was stored in the experimental platform (experiment.html). These differ from the values reported in Table 3 of the paper; the HTML is the authoritative source because it is what was logged in participant CSV files.

tasks.notes: Under the pseudo-syntax, parentheses in the expression are preserved in the output as grouping markers. Option 4 is the naive evaluation result that ignores the grouping display rule.

tasks.domain: Address formatting with reordered variables and literal parentheses
distractor_types: original variable order instead of template order

tasks.expression: "Hello " + name + ", your score is " + score + " out of " + total + "."
options: "Hello name, your score is score out of total."
"Hello Daniel, your 50 is score out of total."
"Hello Daniel, your score is 50 out of 100."
"Hello Daniel, your score is 100 out of 50."
tasks.correct_output: Hello Daniel, your score is 50 out of 100.

options: "Hello Daniel, your score is 50 out of 100."
distractor_types: correct values but wrong template order
correct order but score replaced with total

tasks.domain: Complex arithmetic-style expression with nested grouping
tasks.notes: Under the pseudo-syntax, numeric values are not arithmetically evaluated; they are treated as literal tokens. Parenthesized subexpressions are displayed with their grouping parentheses preserved in the output. Therefore (1+1+1+1) renders as (1111) and (6+7) renders as (67). This differs from standard Python/Java semantics where (1+1+1+1)=4 and (6+7)=13.

tasks.domain: Complex interpolation with nested grouping and quoted literal
distractor_types: partial interpolation — inner braces not resolved
all grouping structure and spacing removed
tasks.notes: The pseudo-syntax used in this experiment is language-neutral and does not correspond to any specific language runtime. Nested interpolation markers {(...)} are valid in this pseudo-syntax: the outer {} triggers interpolation and the inner () marks a group whose contents are also interpolated. This would not compile in Python or similar languages, but is intentional here to test comprehension of nested structure without language-specific bias.

tasks.domain: Variable assignment display with non-sequential order
distractor_types: alphabetical variable order instead of expression order

tasks.domain: Variable assignment display with aliased placeholders
options: "a = a b = b c = b d = c"
distractor_types: values in alphabetical variable order instead of template order
interpolation not applied — braces shown literally
variable names shown instead of values
tasks.notes: This task deliberately aliases label names to different variables (e.g., label 'b' uses variable {d}) to test careful tracking of placeholder-to-variable mappings.

This task tests comprehension of concatenation across a complex mathematical expression. The '+' inside the literal strings does not represent concatenation — only the outer '+' operators between quoted segments do. The expression also includes symbolic variables (m, n, l) that are not defined, requiring participants to treat them as literal tokens.

distractor_types: irrelevant variables a and b substituted instead of userName
path segments reordered (userName appended at end)
path segments reordered (userName inserted before Users)
tasks.notes: Variables a and b are declared but not referenced in the expression, serving as distractors to increase working memory load.

distractor_types: wrong separator style (backslash) and wrong variable values
tasks.notes: Variable a is declared but not referenced. Option 4 uses backslash separators to test whether participants conflate this with Task 13.

tasks.domain: URL construction with partial literal template
distractor_types: path variable incorrectly interpolated where literal 'path' appears
protocol and path variables interpolated (wrong — they are literal in template)
all variables including literal text interpolated
tasks.notes: Only {domain} and {query} are interpolation placeholders. The words 'protocol' and 'path' in the template string are plain text, not placeholders. This tests whether participants distinguish between literal text and interpolation markers.
